question: In Mongolia, how many years longer was female than male life expectancy at birth in 2019?
answer: In Mongolia in 2019, the female life expectancy at birth was 72.8 years and the male life expectancy at birth was 63.8 years [who-whs-2023-p100-table-000]. Female life expectancy was 9.0 years longer than male life expectancy [who-whs-2023-p100-table-000].

question: What proportion of births in Brazil were attended by skilled health personnel?
answer: A total of 98% of births in Brazil were attended by skilled health personnel [who-whs-2023-p097-table-001].

events.query: Brazil births attended by skilled health personnel proportion

results.text:
The assistance of skilled health personnel during childbirth is crucial for the lives of women, their newborns and families. The global coverage of this service increased from 81% in 2015 to an estimated 86% in 2022 (53). The WHO African Region continues to have the lowest coverage of skilled birth attendance across all WHO regions. To accelerate progress, it is essential to ensure that there are enough skilled health

received during the visits or if the women saw a skilled health provider such as a doctor or nurse. The data used to calculate this latter indicator primarily come from household surveys which do capture the type of provider seen on the first ANC visit. From these data, it is estimated that 88% of pregnant women attended at least one ANC visit with a skilled provider between 2015 and 2021. This does not directly indicate the degree to which respectful, quality pregnancy care was received but rather shows an increased likelihood that quality care – which included the recommended interventions for pregnant women – was received from a skilled health provider (versus from a non-skilled provider).

[Vision description] This is a grouped bar chart showing the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older, by WHO regions and globally, for the years 2000 and 2020.

The chart has three panels, stacked vertically, representing "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female".
The y-axis for all panels is "Prevalence (%)", ranging from 0 to 70 in increments of 10.
The x-axis for each panel shows different WHO regions: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.

**Main comparisons and trends:**
*   For "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female", the prevalence of tobacco use decreased in all WHO regions and globally from 2000 to 2020.
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Both sexes" was in the South-East Asia Region (50.4%), and the lowest was in the African Region (17.9%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Male" was in the South-East Asia Region (68.2%), and the lowest was in the African Region (28.7%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Female" was in the South-East Asia Region (32.5%), and the lowest was in the African Region (7.1%) and Western Pacific Region (5.0%).
*   In all regions and globally, male prevalence of tobacco use was significantly higher than female prevalence in both 2000 and 2020.

The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Notwithstanding the progress made in many parts of the world since 2000, the rate of reduction in the prevalence has slowed in 2010–2020 compared to 2000–2010. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Source: Ref. (28).
[Vision description] **Type of figure:** Stacked area chart showing global prevalence of anaemia (%) by severity level among women aged 15–49 years from 2000 to 2019.

**Axes and Legend:**
* **Y-axis:** Anaemia prevalence (%) ranging from 0 to 50 in increments of 5.
* **X-axis:** Years from 2000 to 2019.
* **Legend categories (severity levels):**
  * Severe anaemia (Red)
  * Moderate anaemia (Yellow)
  * Mild anaemia (Blue)

**Printed Data Values:**

* **Severe anaemia (red series):**
  * 2000: 1.7%
  * 2015: 1.1%
  * 2019: 1.0%

* **Moderate anaemia (yellow series):**
  * 2000: 14.1%
  * 2015: 12.2%
  * 2019: 12.7%

* **Mild anaemia (blue series):**
  * 2000: 15.5%
  * 2015: 15.5%
  * 2019: 16.2%

*(Note: Data values for years 2001 through 2014 and 2016 through 2018 are not explicitly labelled on the chart.)*

**Main Comparisons and Trends:**
* **Mild anaemia** accounts for the largest proportion of total prevalence throughout the period, followed by **moderate anaemia**, while **severe anaemia** makes up the smallest proportion.
* **Severe anaemia** shows a slight downward trend over time, declining from 1.7% in 2000 to 1.1% in 2015 and 1.0% in 2019.
* **Moderate anaemia** decreases from 14.1% in 2000 to a low of 12.2% in 2015 before rising slightly to 12.7% in 2019.
* **Mild anaemia** remains steady at 15.5% between 2000 and 2015, then increases to 16.2% in 2019.
* Total overall anaemia prevalence (the top of the stacked area) slightly decreases from 2000 through around 2012–2014 before rising again toward 2019.

Although the global prevalence of anaemia in women aged 15–49 years decreased slightly from 2000 [31.2% (UI: 28.7–34.1)] to 2019 [29.9% (UI: 27.0–32.8)], the total number affected increased considerably due to population growth – from 492.9 million in 2000 to 570.8 million in 2019. Prevalence was higher among pregnant women [36.5% (UI: 34.0–39.1)] than non-pregnant women [29.6% UI: 26.6–32.5)]. Globally, the prevalence of mild anaemia increased slightly from 15.5% (UI: 14.2–17.3) in 2000 to 16.2% (UI: 14.9–17.6) in 2019, while moderate anaemia declined slightly from 14.1% (UI: 12.4–16.1) in 2000 to 12.7% (UI: 10.6–14.8) in 2019, as did severe anaemia
from 1.7% (UI: 1.4–2.0) in 2000 to 1% (UI: 0.8–1.4) in 2019, indicating a shift towards mild anaemia (Figure 2.9) (28).

Across WHO regions, there were declines in the prevalence of total anaemia during the MDG era, but these either slowed or halted after 2015. Between 2000 and 2019, in the WHO Western Pacific Region, anaemia prevalence fell from 22.6% (UI: 16.3–30.4) to 16.4% (UI: 11.4–23.5), in the African Region it fell from 46.3% (UI: 42.5–50) to 40.4% (UI: 36.7–44.2) and in the Region of the Americas from 19.2% (UI: 16.1–22.5) to 15.4% (UI: 12.1–19.5). The prevalence of anaemia continued to be highest in the South-East Asia Region, 46.6% (UI: 39.4–53.1) in 2019. Mild anaemia prevalence slightly increased in the South-East Asia Region from 21% (UI: 19.1–22.8) in 2000 to 23.5% (UI: 20.6–26.0) in 2019 and in the Eastern Mediterranean Region from 18.4 (UI: 16.3–20.7) to 19.6 (UI: 16.5–22.6). In the same period, moderate and severe anaemia declined in all WHO regions.

Although the global prevalence of anaemia in women aged 15–49 years decreased slightly from 2000 [31.2% (UI: 28.7–34.1)] to 2019 [29.9% (UI: 27.0–32.8)], the total number affected increased considerably due to population growth – from 492.9 million in 2000 to 570.8 million in 2019. Prevalence was higher among pregnant women [36.5% (UI: 34.0–39.1)] than non-pregnant women [29.6% UI: 26.6–32.5)]. Globally, the prevalence of mild anaemia increased slightly from 15.5% (UI: 14.2–17.3) in 2000 to 16.2% (UI: 14.9–17.6) in 2019, while moderate anaemia declined slightly from 14.1% (UI: 12.4–16.1) in 2000 to 12.7% (UI: 10.6–14.8) in 2019, as did severe anaemia
from 1.7% (UI: 1.4–2.0) in 2000 to 1% (UI: 0.8–1.4) in 2019, indicating a shift towards mild anaemia (Figure 2.9) (28).

Across WHO regions, there were declines in the prevalence of total anaemia during the MDG era, but these either slowed or halted after 2015. Between 2000 and 2019, in the WHO Western Pacific Region, anaemia prevalence fell from 22.6% (UI: 16.3–30.4) to 16.4% (UI: 11.4–23.5), in the African Region it fell from 46.3% (UI: 42.5–50) to 40.4% (UI: 36.7–44.2) and in the Region of the Americas from 19.2% (UI: 16.1–22.5) to 15.4% (UI: 12.1–19.5). The prevalence of anaemia continued to be highest in the South-East Asia Region, 46.6% (UI: 39.4–53.1) in 2019. Mild anaemia prevalence slightly increased in the South-East Asia Region from 21% (UI: 19.1–22.8) in 2000 to 23.5% (UI: 20.6–26.0) in 2019 and in the Eastern Mediterranean Region from 18.4 (UI: 16.3–20.7) to 19.6 (UI: 16.5–22.6). In the same period, moderate and severe anaemia declined in all WHO regions.

results.text: In 2014, Viet Nam introduced early essential newborn care (EENC), a package of evidence-based interventions that are applied at birth to prevent or manage common causes of newborn morbidity and mortality. These include immediate and thorough drying, sustained skin-to-skin contact, delayed cord clamping, promotion of early and exclusive breastfeeding, resuscitation of non-breathing babies and “kangaroo mother care” (KMC). The core of this approach is sustained skin-to-skin contact between mother and baby (“the first embrace”), which transfers warmth and promotes non-separation.

• Box 1.1 A “first embrace” after caesarean section in Viet Nam is saving newborn lives (5)
Efforts to improve outcomes for mothers and babies in Viet Nam have been increasingly complicated by an accelerating caesarean section rate, estimated at 29% nationally in 2022. Across Viet Nam, babies born by caesarean section are routinely separated from their mothers and admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) for prolonged observation and are given infant formula. This often unnecessary practice has increased the risk of newborn infections and other complications and has resulted in crowded NICUs.

The Da Nang Hospital for Women and Children was one of the first to introduce EENC in Viet Nam, using staff coaching, quality improvement assessments and changes in protocols and environments. After introducing EENC with routine vaginal births, the hospital then pioneered this approach to care with caesarean births by developing methods for coaching surgical teams and improving availability of baby hats, drying cloths and resuscitation areas in operating rooms.
Following this, over the period 2013–2015, data on 16 927 newborns delivered by caesarean section before and after the introduction of EENC showed that total NICU admissions decreased from 16.7% to 11.8% (relative risk 0.71; 95% CI 0.66–0.76). In addition, compared with the pre-EENC period, the number of babies with hypothermia on admission to the NICU declined from 5.0% to 3.7% (relative risk 0.73; 95% CI 0.63–0.84) and cases of sepsis decreased from 3.2% to 0.8% (relative risk 0.26; 95% CI 0.20–0.33).

In 2014, Viet Nam introduced early essential newborn care (EENC), a package of evidence-based interventions that are applied at birth to prevent or manage common causes of newborn morbidity and mortality. These include immediate and thorough drying, sustained skin-to-skin contact, delayed cord clamping, promotion of early and exclusive breastfeeding, resuscitation of non-breathing babies and “kangaroo mother care” (KMC). The core of this approach is sustained skin-to-skin contact between mother and baby (“the first embrace”), which transfers warmth and promotes non-separation.

[who-whs-2023-p021-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 21]
• Box 1.1 A “first embrace” after caesarean section in Viet Nam is saving newborn lives (5)
Efforts to improve outcomes for mothers and babies in Viet Nam have been increasingly complicated by an accelerating caesarean section rate, estimated at 29% nationally in 2022. Across Viet Nam, babies born by caesarean section are routinely separated from their mothers and admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) for prolonged observation and are given infant formula. This often unnecessary practice has increased the risk of newborn infections and other complications and has resulted in crowded NICUs.

[Vision description] **Type of figure:** Timeline infographic (S-curved path depicting public health milestones from 1948 to 2023).

**Data values (Year: Event details):**

* **1948:** WHO Constitution comes into force
* **1974:** WHO founds the Expanded Programme on Immunization to bring life-saving vaccines to all the world's children
* **1978:** 
  * WHO launches the global diarrhoeal diseases programme with oral rehydration salts at its heart
  * The International Conference on Primary Health Care, in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan, sets the aspirational goal, "Health for All", laying the groundwork for WHO's call for UHC
* **1980:** Following an ambitious 12-year global vaccination campaign led by WHO, smallpox is eradicated
* **1988:** The Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI), is launched
* **1999:** The first global strategy for the prevention and control of NCDs
* **2000:** The WHO Global Outbreak Alert and Response Network (GOARN) is established to detect and combat the international spread of outbreaks
* **2003:** 
  * The World Health Assembly unanimously adopts WHO's first global public health treaty, the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control
  * WHO launches the "3 by 5" initiative, which aims to bring treatment to 3 million people living with HIV by 2005 and lays the groundwork for reaching 13 million people infected with HIV with ART by 2013
* **2004:** WHO co-established the UN Road Safety Collaboration to prevent road traffic injuries
* **2005:** The International Health Regulations are revised
* **2006:** WHO Child Growth Standards are launched to help every child grow in an equitable way
* **2012:** The World Health Assembly adopts WHO's implementation plan on maternal, infant, and young child nutrition
* **2014:** The Every Newborn Action Plan is endorsed by the World Health Assembly
* **2015:** All United Nations Member States adopt the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development
* **2019:** UN Declaration on UHC
* **2020:** Access to COVID-19 Tools Accelerator
* **2021:** 
  * More than 74 million lives had been saved through tuberculosis (TB) prevention, diagnosis and treatment since 2000
  * HIV treatment coverage expanded rapidly with well over 17 million people living with HIV on ART by the end of 2015
* **2022:** Agreement for cooperation on the health of humans, animals, plants and the environment
* **2023:** WHO's 75th anniversary

**Main trends:** The graphic displays chronological milestones in WHO's 75-year history, starting from its constitution in 1948 and ending with its 75th anniversary in 2023.

Also important are advancements in medical science and developments in cost-effective policy interventions. For example, the discovery of antibiotics and WHO’s advice to countries on their responsive use since the 1950s have saved hundreds of millions of lives. Similarly, the emergence of many vaccines and mass global vaccination campaigns have led to some of the greatest public health successes, including eradication of smallpox and near eradication of polio, as well as avoiding 3.5–5 million deaths from diseases such as diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, influenza and measles (4).
Since its establishment, WHO has spearheaded many programmes and global action plans that have contributed greatly to improved population health. (Figure 3.3) (5).
Building on past achievements to prepare for the next stage of global health
Building on past achievements to prepare for the next stage of global health 03.

•3.1 Improvements in overall population health over the last seven decades
1 Unless otherwise noted, data on life expectancy, causes of death and burden of disease in this section are derived from the Global Health Estimates 2000–2019 (GHE2019) and World population prospects: 2022 revision (WPP2022). Given the overall good comparability of the two datasets at global and regional levels, the estimates from GHE2019 are used where possible and those from WPP2022 are used in supplement to enable trend analysis for historical (1950–1999) and future years (2020–2048) that are not covered in GHE2019.
Since the foundation of WHO in 1948, the world has experienced countless public health challenges that threatened our health and well-being. However, numerous obstacles have been dismantled and remarkable advancements made in medical science, health care and overall population health.

* **2005:** The International Health Regulations are revised
* **2006:** WHO Child Growth Standards are launched to help every child grow in an equitable way

* **2019:** UN Declaration on UHC

[Vision description] This is a choropleth map titled "Figure 1.2 Maternal mortality ratio by country/area, 2020".

The map displays the maternal mortality ratio (per 100 000 live births) for countries and areas worldwide in 2020.

The legend categories for the maternal mortality ratio are:
- ≥1000 (dark red)
- 500–999 (red)
- 300–499 (dark pink)
- 100–299 (medium pink)
- 20–99 (light pink)
- <20 (very light pink)
- No data available (light grey)
- Not applicable (grey)

A scale bar indicates distances in kilometers: 0, 1000, 2000, 4000 km.

The highest maternal mortality ratios (≥1000, dark red) are concentrated in Central Africa, including countries like Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan, and Somalia. Other countries in this category include Afghanistan and Yemen.

Countries with ratios between 500–999 (red) are also predominantly in Africa, such as Niger, Mali, Nigeria, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Sudan. Some countries in South Asia, like Pakistan, also fall into this category.

The lowest maternal mortality ratios (<20, very light pink) are observed across North America (Canada, United States), most of Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and parts of East Asia (e.g., Japan, South Korea). Many countries in South America also show lower ratios, generally in the 20–99 or 100–299 range.

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland, Western Sahara, and some parts of Central Asia. "Not applicable" (grey) is shown for areas like the Arctic.

Overall, the map clearly shows a strong geographical disparity, with the highest maternal mortality ratios concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia, while North America, Europe, and Oceania generally have the lowest ratios.

Main comparisons and trends:
- The South-East Asia Region had the highest ARR from 2000–2015 (6.1%) and also the highest positive ARR from 2016–2020 (4.5%).
- The European Region had the highest ARR from 2000–2015 among regions with negative ARR in 2016-2020.
- The Region of the Americas had the most negative ARR from 2016–2020 (-3.6%).
- The African Region had the highest MMR in both 2000 (790) and 2020 (540).
- The European Region had the lowest MMR in both 2000 (20) and 2020 (10).
- All regions showed a decrease in MMR from 2000 to 2020.
- European Region, Western Pacific Region, and Region of the Americas experienced a negative ARR from 2016–2020, indicating an increase in maternal mortality during this period.

The maternal mortality ratio levels, as well as the rates of progress and slowdown, have been uneven across WHO regions (Figure 1.1). The WHO South-East Asia Region maintained the fastest reduction rate during the MDG era and the first five years of the SDG era, reducing the maternal mortality ratio from 372 (UI: 336–423) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2000 to 117 (UI: 106–133) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2020. The African Region, while keeping the ARR relatively stable at 2.0% for the past two decades, continued to have the highest maternal mortality ratio. The Region of the Americas, the Western Pacific Region and the European Region saw a trend reversal, with the maternal mortality ratio levels increasing
between 2016 and 2020 after having decreased during the MDG era. However, the levels of the maternal mortality ratio have remained low (below 100 deaths per 100 000 maternal deaths) since 2000.

U5MR and NMR also varied greatly by country/area (Figure 1.6). As of 2021, 133 countries and areas already met the SDG target for U5MR and 126 countries and areas met the target for NMR. Children around the world face vastly different chances of survival depending on where they are born. While U5MR in the African Region fell by 52% between 2000 and 2021, it remained the highest at 72 (UI: 65–84) deaths per 1000 live births – almost twice the global U5MR and about nine times higher that of the European Region which was eight (UI: 7–8) deaths per 1000 live births. Despite a 34% drop in NMR from 40 (UI: 39–42) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000 to 27 (UI: 24–31) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, the number of neonatal deaths in the African Region remained stubbornly high at about 1.1 million annually since 2000 (Figure 1.5), owing to the increasing number of live births. Children around the world face vastly different chances of survival depending on where they are born. Protect health from the wide range of impacts of climate change
Countries are facing increasing threats to public health and health systems from climate change. A number of factors, including geography and socioeconomic conditions influence these risks. Countries can assess their individual health vulnerabilities and capacities and develop evidence-based NAPs and interventions. Climate-informed health surveillance and early warning systems and climate-informed health policies and programmes are critical in strengthening the resilience of health systems to growing climate risks (52).

Build better, more climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable health systems
Building climate-resilient and sustainable health systems involves a systematic and comprehensive approach to strengthening all core functions of a health system so that it can respond and adapt to the health risks of climate change. The 2021 WHO Health and Climate Change Global Survey found that approximately half of countries (48 out of 95) reported having conducted a climate change and health vulnerability and adaptation assessment. Fifty-two per cent (49 out of 95) of countries reported having a national climate change and health strategy or plan in place (Figure 1.16). However, only a quarter of those countries (11 out of 46) have reached a “high” or “very high” level of implementation. Protect health from the wide range of impacts of climate change
Countries are facing increasing threats to public health and health systems from climate change. A number of factors, including geography and socioeconomic conditions influence these risks. Countries can assess their individual health vulnerabilities and capacities and develop evidence-based NAPs and interventions. Climate-informed health surveillance and early warning systems and climate-informed health policies and programmes are critical in strengthening the resilience of health systems to growing climate risks (52).
Given the interconnectedness of natural, economic, social and human systems, action in the health sector alone is not enough to protect human health. As climate change intensifies,

[who-whs-2023-p038-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 38]
Build better, more climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable health systems
Building climate-resilient and sustainable health systems involves a systematic and comprehensive approach to strengthening all core functions of a health system so that it can respond and adapt to the health risks of climate change. The 2021 WHO Health and Climate Change Global Survey found that approximately half of countries (48 out of 95) reported having conducted a climate change and health vulnerability and adaptation assessment. Fifty-two per cent (49 out of 95) of countries reported having a national climate change and health strategy or plan in place (Figure 1.16). However, only a quarter of those countries (11 out of 46) have reached a “high” or “very high” level of implementation. Insufficient finance was a main barrier to implementation of national strategies and plans (Figure 1.17) (48).

Continued improvements were made towards the treatment targets for HIV,4 despite the COVID-19 pandemic. The HIV testing and treatment cascade (Figure 2.20) shows that in 2021, an estimated 85% (UI: 75–97%) of the 38.4 (UI: 33.9–43.8) million people living with HIV (PLHIV) globally knew their HIV status, 75% (UI: 66 – 85%) of PLHIV were on HIV treatment, and 68% (UI: 60–78%) of PLHIV were virally suppressed, a marked improvement since 2015. [Vision description] Figure 2.1 is a two-panel line chart showing new HIV infections per 1000 uninfected population from 2000 to 2021.

Panel a. WHO regions (excluding Africa) and global.
The y-axis represents new HIV infections (per 1000 uninfected population), ranging from 0 to 0.5. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021.
Legend categories are: Region of the Americas (light blue), Eastern Mediterranean Region (green), European Region (orange), South-East Asia Region (purple), Western Pacific Region (yellow), and Global (dark purple).

Trends:
*   Global (dark purple line) shows a consistent decrease from approximately 0.48 in 2000 to about 0.26 in 2021.
*   South-East Asia Region (purple line) shows a decrease from approximately 0.28 in 2000 to about 0.08 in 2021.
*   Region of the Americas (light blue line) shows a relatively stable trend, starting around 0.22 in 2000 and ending around 0.18 in 2021.
*   European Region (orange line) shows an initial decrease, then an increase from around 2007, ending around 0.18 in 2021.
*   Eastern Mediterranean Region (green line) and Western Pacific Region (yellow line) show the lowest rates, both remaining below 0.1 throughout the period, with the Western Pacific Region slightly higher than the Eastern Mediterranean Region.

Panel b. WHO African Region, eastern and southern Africa, western and central Africa and global.
The y-axis represents new HIV infections (per 1000 uninfected population), ranging from 0 to 6.0. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021.
Legend categories are: African Region (red), Eastern and southern Africa (light green), Western and central Africa (yellow), and Global (purple).

Trends:
*   Eastern and southern Africa (light green line) shows the highest rates, decreasing significantly from approximately 5.9 in 2000 to about 1.6 in 2021.
*   African Region (red line) shows a decrease from approximately 3.2 in 2000 to about 0.9 in 2021.
*   Western and central Africa (yellow line) shows a decrease from approximately 1.4 in 2000 to about 0.5 in 2021.
*   Global (purple line) shows the lowest rates in this panel, decreasing from approximately 0.5 in 2000 to about 0.26 in 2021.

Overall, all regions and global trends show a decrease in new HIV infections from 2000 to 2021, with African regions having significantly higher rates compared to other WHO regions.

In June 2021, the UN General Assembly adopted the Political Declaration on HIV and AIDS: Ending Inequalities and Getting on Track to End AIDS by 2030. The core targets require a decrease in annual global new HIV infections to less than 370 000 and HIV-related deaths to fewer than 250 000 by 2025. Latest data available show that despite service disruptions caused by the global COVID-19 pandemic, new HIV infections and HIV-related deaths continued to decline – though not for everyone and not everywhere (1).

Figure 2.7 consists of two line charts side by side, showing global data for children under 5 years of age from 2000 to 2022. Both charts feature horizontal x-axes labeled with years (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2022).

**Data Values**

*Prevalence (%) of children under 5 years affected:*
* Stunting: 2000 = 33.0%; 2022 = 22.3%
* Overweight: 2000 = 5.3%; 2022 = 5.6%
* Wasting: 2022 = 6.8% (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

*Number (millions) of children under 5 years affected:*
* Stunting: 2000 = 204.2 million; 2005 = 197.1 million; 2010 = 184.8 million; 2015 = 169.1 million; 2022 = 148.1 million
* Overweight: 2000 = 33.0 million; 2005 = 35.5 million; 2010 = 36.2 million; 2015 = 38.0 million; 2022 = 37.0 million
* Wasting: 2022 = 45.0 million (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

**Main Trends and Comparisons**
* **Stunting:** Decreased steadily between 2000 and 2022 in both prevalence (from 33.0% to 22.3%) and total numbers (from 204.2 million to 148.1 million). It remains the highest category among the three conditions throughout the period.
* **Overweight:** Remained relatively stable in prevalence, slightly rising from 5.3% in 2000 to 5.6% in 2022. The total number increased from 33.0 million in 2000 to a peak labeled value of 38.0 million in 2015, before slightly dropping to 37.0 million in 2022.
* **Wasting:** Data is only labeled for 2022, standing at a prevalence of 6.8% and affecting 45.0 million children.

Stunting
Stunting is the result of chronic and recurrent malnutrition in mothers and in children who do not grow to their maximum potential.
The global prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years of age fell from 33.0% (UI: 32.4–33.5) in 2000 to 22.3% (UI: 21.8–22.9) in 2022. The decline occurred more rapidly during the MDG era, with an ARR of 2.0% between 2000 and 2015 – spurred by the rapid decline during the second half of the period – compared to the decline since the start of the SDG era in 2015, with an ARR of 1.4%.
Stunting prevalence also declined in all WHO regions, albeit at different paces (Figure 2.8). In both the European and the Western Pacific regions, prevalence fell by more than half between 2000 and 2022, but the progress slowed in the
Western Pacific Region in the more recent period. In contrast, prevalence reduction has gathered speed in the South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean regions in the second half of the MDG era.

Still, in 2022, there were 49.8 million children under 5 years of age affected by stunting in the South-East Asia Region [30.1% (UI: 28.3–32.0)], 56.2 million in the African Region [31.0% (UI: 30.2–31.8)] and 22.9 million in the Eastern Mediterranean Region [25.1% (UI: 23.4–26.8)].
Globally, an estimated 148.1 million children under 5 years of age were affected by stunting in 2022. These numbers may become substantially higher as the global food and nutrition crisis continues to unfold – fueled by conflict, climate change and the enduring effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The full impact of the crisis on stunting may take years to manifest (27).

* **Stunting:** Decreased steadily between 2000 and 2022 in both prevalence (from 33.0% to 22.3%) and total numbers (from 204.2 million to 148.1 million). It remains the highest category among the three conditions throughout the period.
* **Overweight:** Remained relatively stable in prevalence, slightly rising from 5.3% in 2000 to 5.6% in 2022. The total number increased from 33.0 million in 2000 to a peak labeled value of 38.0 million in 2015, before slightly dropping to 37.0 million in 2022.
* **Wasting:** Data is only labeled for 2022, standing at a prevalence of 6.8% and affecting 45.0 million children.

[who-whs-2023-p058-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 58]
Stunting
Stunting is the result of chronic and recurrent malnutrition in mothers and in children who do not grow to their maximum potential.
The global prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years of age fell from 33.0% (UI: 32.4–33.5) in 2000 to 22.3% (UI: 21.8–22.9) in 2022. The decline occurred more rapidly during the MDG era, with an ARR of 2.0% between 2000 and 2015 – spurred by the rapid decline during the second half of the period – compared to the decline since the start of the SDG era in 2015, with an ARR of 1.4%.
Stunting prevalence also declined in all WHO regions, albeit at different paces (Figure 2.8). In both the European and the Western Pacific regions, prevalence fell by more than half between 2000 and 2022, but the progress slowed in the
Western Pacific Region in the more recent period. In contrast, prevalence reduction has gathered speed in the South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean regions in the second half of the MDG era.

[who-whs-2023-p058-text-001 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 58]
Still, in 2022, there were 49.8 million children under 5 years of age affected by stunting in the South-East Asia Region [30.1% (UI: 28.3–32.0)], 56.2 million in the African Region [31.0% (UI: 30.2–31.8)] and 22.9 million in the Eastern Mediterranean Region [25.1% (UI: 23.4–26.8)].
Globally, an estimated 148.1 million children under 5 years of age were affected by stunting in 2022. These numbers may become substantially higher as the global food and nutrition crisis continues to unfold – fueled by conflict, climate change and the enduring effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The full impact of the crisis on stunting may take years to manifest (27).

Observations:
*   Many data points from the African Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region, South-East Asia Region, and Western Pacific Region are clustered in the lower-left quadrant, generally below 100 for both crude and age-standardized rates.

For instance, there are European Region points with crude rates around 300-400 and age-standardized rates around 100-200.
*   The highest crude excess death rates (approaching 400-450) are observed in the European Region, with corresponding age-standardized rates around 150-250.
*   The highest age-standardized excess death rates (approaching 350) are observed in the European Region, with corresponding crude rates around 250-300.

For instance, countries with older population structures might have a higher excess mortality rate because COVID-19 disproportionately affects the populations that are frailer and in older age groups. Seventy-five of WHO’s 194 Member States have a crude excess mortality rate higher than the agestandardized excess mortality rate, indicating a much older population structure. These countries come predominantly from the Region of Americas and the European Region. Fortysix of the 53 Member States in the European Region have an age-standardized excess mortality rate lower than the crude excess mortality rate. In the Region of the Americas, 15 of the 35 Member States have seen an age-standardized excess mortality rate lower than the crude excess mortality rate. On the other hand, few countries in the African Region and the Eastern Mediterranean Region (only 1 and 2 respectively) have seen crude excess mortality rates higher than the agestandardized values (Figure 1.14).

question: What was the prevalence of current tobacco use among males in the South-East Asia Region in 2000 and in 2020?
answer: The age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among males in the South-East Asia Region was 68.2% in 2000 and 46.6% in 2020 [who-whs-2023-p025-fig1.9].

[Vision description] This is a grouped bar chart showing the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older, by WHO regions and globally, for the years 2000 and 2020.

The chart has three panels, stacked vertically, representing "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female".
The y-axis for all panels is "Prevalence (%)", ranging from 0 to 70 in increments of 10.
The x-axis for each panel shows different WHO regions: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.
Within each region/global category, there are two bars: a blue bar representing the year 2000 and an orange bar representing the year 2020.

**Main comparisons and trends:**
*   For "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female", the prevalence of tobacco use decreased in all WHO regions and globally from 2000 to 2020.
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Both sexes" was in the South-East Asia Region (50.4%), and the lowest was in the African Region (17.9%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Male" was in the South-East Asia Region (68.2%), and the lowest was in the African Region (28.7%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Female" was in the South-East Asia Region (32.5%), and the lowest was in the African Region (7.1%) and Western Pacific Region (5.0%).
*   In all regions and globally, male prevalence of tobacco use was significantly higher than female prevalence in both 2000 and 2020.

The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Notwithstanding the progress made in many parts of the world since 2000, the rate of reduction in the prevalence has slowed in 2010–2020 compared to 2000–2010. question: In the African Region in 2020, what proportion of the population used safely-managed drinking-water, safely-managed sanitation and a hand-washing facility with soap and water?
answer: In the African Region in 2020, the proportion of the population that used safely-managed drinking-water services was 32%, safely-managed sanitation services was 23%, and a hand-washing facility with soap and water was 28% [who-whs-2023-p066-fig2.13].

results.text: Substantial global progress has been made in reducing child mortality since 2000. Approximately 10 million (9.9 million, UI: 9.8–10.1 million)2 children under 5 years of age died globally in 2000, corresponding to an under-five mortality rate (U5MR) of 76 (UI: 75–78) deaths per 1000 live births. Both the global number of deaths and the U5MR halved by 2021 (Figure 1.4). However, 5.0 million (UI: 4.8–5.6 million) children in 2021 tragically died before reaching their fifth birthday. Just under half (47%) of these deaths – about 2.3 million (UI: 2.2–2.6 million) – occurred during the first month of life. The global neonatal mortality rate (NMR) stood at 18 (UI: 17–19) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, a 43% drop from 31 (UI: 30–32) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000. The global U5MR in 2021 was 38 (UI: 36–42) deaths per 1000 live births (4).

U5MR and NMR also varied greatly by country/area (Figure 1.6). As of 2021, 133 countries and areas already met the SDG target for U5MR and 126 countries and areas met the target for NMR. However, in 14 countries U5MR was over 75 per 1000 live births, and in 29 countries NMR was over 25 deaths per 1000 live births.

[Vision description] This is a choropleth map titled "Figure 1.6 Under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, by country/area, 2021". The map displays two types of mortality rates for countries and areas worldwide in 2021.

The "Under-five mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" is represented by color-coded regions:
- >75: Dark purple
- 51-75: Purple
- 26-50: Pink
- ≤25: Light orange
- No data available: Light grey
- Not applicable: Dark grey

The "Neonatal mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" is represented by circles of varying sizes and colors:
- 40: Largest red circle
- 29: Medium red circle
- 18: Small red circle
- 12: Medium green circle
- 1: Smallest green circle

The map shows that countries in sub-Saharan Africa generally have the highest under-five mortality rates (>75 and 51-75, dark purple and purple regions) and also the highest neonatal mortality rates (largest red circles, 40 and 29). Examples include Chad, Central African Republic, Somalia, and Nigeria.

Conversely, most countries in North America, Europe, Australia, and parts of Asia have the lowest under-five mortality rates (≤25, light orange regions) and the lowest neonatal mortality rates (smallest green circles, 1 and 12). Examples include Canada, United States, most of Western Europe, Australia, and Japan.

Some countries in South Asia and Southeast Asia, such as India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, show a mix of pink (26-50) and light orange (≤25) for under-five mortality, with varying neonatal mortality rates, including some red circles (18 and 29).

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland and parts of the Sahara desert. "Not applicable" (dark grey) is shown for some small island nations and territories.

Children around the world face vastly different chances of survival depending on where they are born. While U5MR in the African Region fell by 52% between 2000 and 2021, it remained the highest at 72 (UI: 65–84) deaths per 1000 live births – almost twice the global U5MR and about nine times higher that of the European Region which was eight (UI: 7–8) deaths per 1000 live births. Despite a 34% drop in NMR from 40 (UI: 39–42) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000 to 27 (UI: 24–31) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, the number of neonatal deaths in the African Region remained stubbornly high at about 1.1 million annually since 2000 (Figure 1.5), owing to the increasing number of live births. The South-East Asia Region saw a big decline in deaths as the number of neonatal and post-neonatal under-five deaths dropped by 65% and 78%, respectively, between 2000 and 2021.

[who-whs-2023-p018-text-001 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 18]
Substantial global progress has been made in reducing child mortality since 2000. Approximately 10 million (9.9 million, UI: 9.8–10.1 million)2 children under 5 years of age died globally in 2000, corresponding to an under-five mortality rate (U5MR) of 76 (UI: 75–78) deaths per 1000 live births. Both the global number of deaths and the U5MR halved by 2021 (Figure 1.4). However, 5.0 million (UI: 4.8–5.6 million) children in 2021 tragically died before reaching their fifth birthday. Just under half (47%) of these deaths – about 2.3 million (UI: 2.2–2.6 million) – occurred during the first month of life. The global neonatal mortality rate (NMR) stood at 18 (UI: 17–19) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, a 43% drop from 31 (UI: 30–32) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000. The global U5MR in 2021 was 38 (UI: 36–42) deaths per 1000 live births (4).

[who-whs-2023-p018-text-004 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 18]
U5MR and NMR also varied greatly by country/area (Figure 1.6). As of 2021, 133 countries and areas already met the SDG target for U5MR and 126 countries and areas met the target for NMR. However, in 14 countries U5MR was over 75 per 1000 live births, and in 29 countries NMR was over 25 deaths per 1000 live births.

Children around the world face vastly different chances of survival depending on where they are born. While U5MR in the African Region fell by 52% between 2000 and 2021, it remained the highest at 72 (UI: 65–84) deaths per 1000 live births – almost twice the global U5MR and about nine times higher that of the European Region which was eight (UI: 7–8) deaths per 1000 live births. Despite a 34% drop in NMR from 40 (UI: 39–42) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000 to 27 (UI: 24–31) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, the number of neonatal deaths in the African Region remained stubbornly high at about 1.1 million annually since 2000 (Figure 1.5), owing to the increasing number of live births. The South-East Asia Region saw a big decline in deaths as the number of neonatal and post-neonatal under-five deaths dropped by 65% and 78%, respectively, between 2000 and 2021.

results.text:
Obesity
The age-standardized prevalence of obesity among adults aged 18 years or older – i.e. body mass index (BMI) >30 kg/m2 – has been rising since the 1970s. In 2016, 13.1% (UI: 12.4–13.9%) of adults globally were obese, up from 8.7% (UI: 8.4–9.0) in 2000. The greatest increases occurred in the South-East Asia Region, up from 1.9% (UI: 1.6–2.2%) to 4.7% (UI: 3.9–5.6%) (an almost 150% increase) and the Western Pacific Region, up from 2.7% (UI: 2.4–3.0%) to 6.4% (UI: 5.2–7.7%) (an almost 140% increase). The highest level of adult obesity is 2016 was in the Americas where 28.6% (UI: 26.6–30.5%) of adults were obese, increasing by 42% from 20.2% (UI: 19.0–21.5%) in 2000 (Figure 1.10) (10).

Main trends and comparisons:
Across all regions and globally, the prevalence of obesity has consistently increased from 1975 to 2016 for both sexes, males, and females.

Region-specific observations (approximate values based on visual estimation, as no specific data labels are provided):

- **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 25%, male around 15%, and both sexes around 20%.
- **European Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 25%, male around 20%, and both sexes around 22%.

- **Western Pacific Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 7%, male around 5%, and both sexes around 6%.
- **Global:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 15%, male around 10%, and both sexes around 12%.

[Vision description] Figure 1.11 is a multi-panel line chart showing the age-standardized prevalence of hypertension among adults (age 30–79 years) across different WHO regions and globally, from 1990 to 2019.

The figure consists of seven panels, each representing a different region or the global average: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.

The y-axis for all panels represents "Prevalence (%)" ranging from 0 to 50 in increments of 5. The x-axis for all panels represents years: 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2019.

The legend indicates three line categories:
- Light blue line: Both sexes
- Orange line: Male
- Purple line: Female

**Observed Trends and Comparisons:**

**African Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then decreased by 2019.
- Female prevalence (purple line) is consistently higher than male prevalence (orange line).
- In 2010, female prevalence peaked at approximately 31%, male at approximately 27%, and both sexes at approximately 29%.

**Region of the Americas:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then decreased by 2019.
- Female prevalence (purple line) is consistently lower than male prevalence (orange line).
- In 2010, male prevalence peaked at approximately 29.5%, female at approximately 24%, and both sexes at approximately 27%.

**Eastern Mediterranean Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then slightly decreased by 2019.
- Female prevalence (purple line) is consistently higher than male prevalence (orange line).
- In 2010, female prevalence peaked at approximately 31%, male at approximately 28%, and both sexes at approximately 29.5%.

**European Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females consistently decreased from 1990 to 2019.
- Male prevalence (orange line) is consistently higher than female prevalence (purple line).
- In 1990, male prevalence was highest at approximately 42%, female at approximately 38%, and both sexes at approximately 40%.
- In 2019, male prevalence was lowest at approximately 34%, female at approximately 22%, and both sexes at approximately 28%. This region shows the most significant decline.

**South-East Asia Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females consistently increased from 1990 to 2019.
- Male prevalence (orange line) is consistently higher than female prevalence (purple line).
- In 2019, male prevalence was highest at approximately 22%, female at approximately 20%, and both sexes at approximately 21%.

**Western Pacific Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then decreased by 2019.
- Male prevalence (orange line) is consistently higher than female prevalence (purple line).
- In 2010, male prevalence peaked at approximately 30%, female at approximately 24%, and both sexes at approximately 27%.

**Global:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then decreased by 2019.
- Male prevalence (orange line) is consistently higher than female prevalence (purple line).
- In 2010, male prevalence peaked at approximately 26%, female at approximately 23%, and both sexes at approximately 24.5%.
- In 2019, male prevalence was approximately 23%, female at approximately 20.5%, and both sexes at approximately 22%.

Overall, the European Region shows a clear downward trend in hypertension prevalence across all categories, while the South-East Asia Region shows a consistent upward trend. Other regions and the global average show an initial increase followed by a decrease. Male prevalence is generally higher than female prevalence in most regions and globally, except for the African and Eastern Mediterranean Regions where female prevalence is higher.

Hypertension
The global age-standardized prevalence of hypertension among adults aged 30–79 years has been rising since 1990 before peaking around 2009; it declined thereafter to 33.1% (UI: 31.5–34.8%) in 2019 (Figure 1.11). events.query: Brazil UHC service coverage index

results.text:
Monitoring the coverage of essential services presents unique challenges due to the inclusionary nature of UHC and its emphasis on providing health services (promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative and palliative) of sufficient quality to be effective to persons in need. No index can fully summarize all the health services required across the life course to achieve UHC. Given this fact, the current UHC Service Coverage Index (UHC SCI) uses a selection of key indicators to track overall coverage of essential health services. The UHC SCI comprises four subindices related to areas of key health concern, namely: reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health (RMNCH); infectious diseases; NCDs; and health service capacity and access. The following paragraphs describe the tracer indicators and related metrics which are used to monitor progress on the pathway to UHC.

•2.5 UHC and health systems
UHC means that all people can get the health services they need, of good quality, and without facing financial hardship from the need to pay for those services. SDG target 3.8 specifically aims to achieve UHC – including financial risk protection, access to quality essential health care services and access to safe, effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all – by 2030. Advances towards this target are tracked through indicators on the coverage of essential health services (SDG 3.8.1), which is a composite index of health service tracer indicators, and one indicator for the lack of financial protection (SDG 3.8.2), which is defined as the proportion of a country’s population with large household expenditures on health relative to their total household expenditure. While assessed separately, both UHC indicators provide vital information about the coverage and cost of health services in countries and need to be tracked together.

Monitoring the coverage of essential services presents unique challenges due to the inclusionary nature of UHC and its emphasis on providing health services (promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative and palliative) of sufficient quality to be effective to persons in need. No index can fully summarize all the health services required across the life course to achieve UHC. Given this fact, the current UHC Service Coverage Index (UHC SCI) uses a selection of key indicators to track overall coverage of essential health services. The UHC SCI comprises four subindices related to areas of key health concern, namely: reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health (RMNCH); infectious diseases; NCDs; and health service capacity and access. question: What share of adults globally were obese in 2016, and how did that compare with 2000?
answer: In 2016, 13.1% (UI: 12.4–13.9%) of adults globally were obese [who-whs-2023-p025-text-000]. This was up from 8.7% (UI: 8.4–9.0) in 2000 [who-whs-2023-p025-text-000].

events.query: share of adults globally obese 2016 2000

results.text:
Obesity
The age-standardized prevalence of obesity among adults aged 18 years or older – i.e. body mass index (BMI) >30 kg/m2 – has been rising since the 1970s. In 2016, 13.1% (UI: 12.4–13.9%) of adults globally were obese, up from 8.7% (UI: 8.4–9.0) in 2000. The greatest increases occurred in the South-East Asia Region, up from 1.9% (UI: 1.6–2.2%) to 4.7% (UI: 3.9–5.6%) (an almost 150% increase) and the Western Pacific Region, up from 2.7% (UI: 2.4–3.0%) to 6.4% (UI: 5.2–7.7%) (an almost 140% increase). question: How many excess deaths globally could be attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic by the end of 2021?
answer: A total of 14.9 million estimated excess deaths was associated with the COVID-19 pandemic globally between 2020 and 2021 [who-whs-2023-p031-text-000].

events.query: excess deaths globally COVID-19 pandemic end of 2021

results.text: The large discrepancy between estimated global excess mortality and the reported deaths due to COVID-19 – a difference of 9.4 million by the end of 2021 – shows that the impact of the pandemic is far-reaching. Indeed, 162 out of 194 WHO Member States show a higher excess mortality rate associated with the COVID-19 pandemic than the reported mortality rate attributable to COVID-19 between 2020 and 2021.

UI: 9.1–12.1 million) – than in 2020 when there was a total of 4.4 million (UI: 3.9–5.0 million). At the regional level, the South- East Asia Region had the highest number of excess deaths for the years 2020 and 2021 at 6.1 million (UI: 4.7–7.8 million), which account for 41% of global excess deaths; this was significantly different from the percentage of globally reported COVID-19 deaths that the South-East Asia Region accounted for over the same period (13.3% of global reported deaths). Except for the Western Pacific Region and the African Region, which had only 0.2 million (UI: 0.0–0.4 million) and 0.8 million (UI: 0.5–1.1 million) estimated excess deaths respectively, all other regions had estimated excess deaths of more than 1 million by the end of 2021. Both the European Region and the Region of the Americas had excess deaths over 3 million – i.e. 3.2 million (UI: 3.1–3.2 million) in Europe and 3.2 million (UI: 3.2–3.3 million) in the Americas (Figure 1.13) (25).

[Vision description] Figure 1.13 is a stacked bar chart showing total excess deaths by WHO region from 1 January 2020 to 31 December 2021.

The y-axis represents "Deaths (in millions)" ranging from 0 to 10.
The x-axis represents different WHO regions: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, and Western Pacific Region.

The legend indicates two categories:
- Light blue: "Reported COVID-19"
- Orange: "Excess deaths not captured in reported COVID-19 deaths"

Each bar represents the total excess deaths for a region, with the total value and uncertainty interval (UI) labelled above the bar. Error bars indicate the uncertainty interval.

Data values are as follows:
- African Region: Total: 0.8 (UI 0.5–1.1) million. Reported COVID-19: 0.2 million.
- Region of the Americas: Total: 3.2 (UI 3.2–3.3) million. Reported COVID-19: 2.4 million.
- Eastern Mediterranean Region: Total: 1.3 (UI 1.1–1.5) million. Reported COVID-19: 0.3 million.
- European Region: Total: 3.2 (UI 3.1–3.2) million. Reported COVID-19: 1.7 million.
- South-East Asia Region: Total: 6.1 (UI 4.7–7.8) million. Reported COVID-19: 0.7 million.
- Western Pacific Region: Total: 0.2 (UI 0–0.4) million. Reported COVID-19: 0.2 million.

Main comparisons:
- The South-East Asia Region has the highest total excess deaths at 6.1 million, with a large proportion of these being excess deaths not captured in reported COVID-19 deaths.
- The Western Pacific Region has the lowest total excess deaths at 0.2 million, with all of these being reported COVID-19 deaths.
- The Region of the Americas and European Region have the second highest total excess deaths, both at 3.2 million.
- For the African Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region, and South-East Asia Region, the orange segment (excess deaths not captured) is significantly larger than the light blue segment (reported COVID-19).
- For the Region of the Americas and European Region, both segments are substantial, with reported COVID-19 deaths being higher in the Americas (2.4 million) than in Europe (1.7 million).
- For the Western Pacific Region, all 0.2 million excess deaths are reported COVID-19 deaths, and there are no excess deaths not captured in reported COVID-19 deaths.

Age and sex distributions in the excess mortality associated with the COVID-19 pandemic
While a total of 14.9 million estimated excess deaths was associated with the COVID-19 pandemic between 2020 and 2021, the age distribution of the COVID-19-related excess mortality shows that the pandemic disproportionally affected the age group of 45 years and above (14.2 million or 95% of the global excess deaths). While 0.7 million excess deaths were observed in the age group of 25–44 years (5% of the global excess deaths), fewer deaths than expected (about 37 000 fewer deaths) were estimated to have occurred among people under the age of 25 years. An estimated 31% of the global excess deaths occurred in ages between 45 and 64 years (i.e. 4.6 million). Similarly, 46% of global excess deaths (i.e. 6.8 million) occurred between 65 and 84 years. The oldest age group, 85 years and above, accounted for 18% of excess deaths globally (i.e. 2.7 million) (25).

Years of life lost due to excess mortality associated with the COVID-19 pandemic
While excess mortality – as opposed to the deaths reported to be due to COVID-19 – provides a unique lens through which to evaluate the toll of the pandemic, it does not comprehensively account for the impact of each death due to the pandemic on a wide range of social and economic issues. Estimation of years of life lost (YLL), on the other hand, accounts not only for the number of deaths and the age at which death occurs but also for the associated loss of a potential number of life‑years. YLL estimates show that a total of 336.8 million life‑years have been lost globally due to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020–2021. This means that, on average, each excess death led to a loss of more than 22 years of life – equivalent to over 5 years of life lost per second in 2020–2021 (25).
Globally, YLL associated with the COVID-19 pandemic is negative among ages younger than 25 years, reflecting YLL averted

question: Since 2016, for how many countries has the availability and affordability of a core set of essential medicines been estimated, and what was the median value?

question: What was the global male-to-female ratio of tobacco use prevalence in 2020, and how had it changed since 2000?
answer: The global male-to-female ratio of tobacco use prevalence was 4.7 in 2020 [who-whs-2023-p024-text-002]. This had risen from 3.0 in 2000, indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women [who-whs-2023-p024-text-002].

events.query: global male-to-female ratio tobacco use prevalence 2020 2000

results.text: The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). (43).
[Vision description] **Figure Type and Layout**
Figure 2.14 is a combination Pareto-style chart featuring blue vertical bar charts (representing Mortality rate) overlaid with a purple line graph (representing Cumulative share of number of deaths) across WHO regions for the year 2019. 

* **Horizontal Axis (WHO regions):** African Region, South-East Asia Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region, Region of the Americas, Western Pacific Region, European Region.
* **Left Vertical Axis (Mortality rate):** Measured in "per 100 000 population", with grid lines spanning from 0 to 50 in increments of 10.
* **Right Vertical Axis (Cumulative share):** Measured in "Cumulative share of number of deaths (%)", with grid lines spanning from 0 to 100% in increments of 20%.
* **Legend:** 
  * Blue bar: Mortality rate
  * Purple line: Cumulative share of number of deaths

**Data Values**
* Individual numerical values for each region's mortality rate and cumulative percentage share are not printed directly as text labels on the chart elements.

**Main Visible Trends and Comparisons**
* **Mortality Rate:** The African Region has the highest mortality rate per 100,000 population, followed by the South-East Asia Region and the Eastern Mediterranean Region. The Region of the Americas, Western Pacific Region, and European Region have substantially lower mortality rates.
* **Cumulative Share of Deaths:** The purple line demonstrates that the top two regions (African Region and South-East Asia Region) account for approximately 80% of the cumulative share of total deaths attributed to exposure to unsafe WASH services.

[Vision description] **Type of Figure:**  
Line chart showing global immunization rates from 2000 to 2021.  
- **X-axis:** Years (2000 through 2021).  
- **Y-axis:** Percentage (%) ranging from 0 to 100 in increments of 20.  
- **Legend / Vaccine Series:** 
  - DTP3 (blue line)
  - HPV (green line)
  - MCV2 (red line)
  - PCV3 (yellow line)

**Data Values:**  
- No explicit numerical labels are printed on individual data points across any of the line series (all values must be read from the y-axis grid lines).

**Main Comparisons and Trends:**  
- **DTP3:** Remains the highest of all four vaccines throughout the entire timeframe (2000–2021), starting above 70% in 2000, peaking near 85–86% between 2015 and 2019, and slightly declining after 2019 to just above 80% in 2021.
- **MCV2:** Shows a steady overall increase from under 20% in 2000 to over 70% by 2020, followed by a slight drop in 2021.
- **PCV3:** Data begins in 2008 at under 10% and increases consistently to around 50% by 2020 and 2021.
- **HPV:** Represents the lowest immunization rate of the group; data begins in 2010 at near 0% and increases gradually to peak slightly above 10% in 2019 before stabilizing around 10% in 2020 and 2021.

results.text:
•2.3 Injuries and violence
Global death rates due to injuries declined by 20% during the period 2000–2019 – from 71.7 (UI: 53.8–93.8) deaths per 100 000 population to 57.4 (UI: 38.7–81.4) deaths per 100 000 population. Over this period, injuries caused about 8% of all deaths. In 2019, deaths due to road traffic injuries made up 29% of all injury deaths, followed by suicide and falls (each causing 16% of all injury deaths), and homicide (11% of all injury deaths) (29).
The suicide rate fell by 29% globally between 2000 and 2019, from 13.0 (UI: 10.4–16.0) to 9.2 (UI: 9.7–12.6) deaths per 100 000 population (Figure 2.11). In all WHO regions, suicide rates have been on the decline, except in the Region of the Americas where the rate rose by 28%. The greatest decline (42%) was seen in the European Region, although the suicide rate in 2019 remained the highest at 12.8 (UI 10.1–16.4) deaths per 100 000 population.

Globally in 2019, an estimated 1.4 million deaths – equivalent to 2.5% of all deaths that year – could have been prevented with safe WASH. These include deaths due to diarrhoea, acute respiratory infections, soil-transmitted helminthiases and undernutrition. Almost all (97%) of these deaths were in low- and middle-income countries, with 79% in the African and South- East Asia regions (Figure 2.14). The African Region suffered the highest mortality rate at 46.7 deaths per 100 000 population – over 10 times the rates in the Western Pacific and European regions. At 29.6 deaths per 100 000, the mortality rate in the South-East Asia Region was 62% higher than the global average of 18.3 deaths per 100 000 population (43).

The global death rate due to homicides declined by 22% over the same period. However, progress varied greatly across WHO regions, with the homicide rate in the European Region declining by 63% while that in the Region of the Americas stayed roughly the same. In 2019, the homicide rate of 19.2 (UI: 15.6–23.7) deaths per 100 000 population in the Region of the Americas was over three times the global average of 6.2 (UI: 4.0–8.7) deaths per 100 000 population).

Globally, men are about twice as likely to die from injury than women are. The death rates due to all injuries in 2019 were 77.6 (UI: 52.7–109.1) deaths per 100 000 male population and 36.9 (UI: 24.4–53.2) deaths per 100 000 female population. Across WHO regions and among the three injury causes discussed in this section, the male-to-female ratio of death rates in 2019 was highest for homicide in the Region of the Americas, where the death rate among men and boys was over seven times that among women and girls.

Unintentional poisoning
Unintentional poisoning can be caused by household chemicals, pesticides, kerosene, carbon monoxide and medicines or may be the result of environmental contamination or occupational chemical exposure. Unintentional poisonings were responsible for about 84 000 (UI: 48 000–137 000) deaths in 2019 – of
which 73% are thought to be preventable through sound chemical management (29,47). Because of occupational exposures, death rates due to unintentional poisonings are higher among men than women, although the gap has narrowed slightly in recent years (Figure 2.17).
